slides.title: Role of Coding Agents in Software Workspaces
bullets: Coding agents automate tasks like refactoring, test execution, and bug fixing.
Agents require controlled access to workspace files and executable development tools.
Context engineering ensures the agent receives precise, structured workspace context.
Integrating tool interfaces extends agent capabilities beyond text generation.
slides.notes: Coding agents act as autonomous collaborators within modern integrated development environments. Unlike basic text completion models, agents can read project files, run test suites, and analyze compilation outputs. However, their performance depends heavily on the quality and structure of context supplied from the workspace. Context engineering provides the necessary boundary definitions, standardizing how context and tool interfaces are supplied to the LLM backend.

slides.title: Fundamentals of Context Engineering
bullets: Context engineering curates prompt instructions, repository state, and dynamic tools.
Token budget limitations demand selective context inclusion over raw repository dumping.
Structured formats like JSON and Markdown help agents parse workspace metadata accurately.
Properly engineered context prevents model hallucination and static analysis errors.
slides.notes: Context engineering goes beyond basic prompt engineering. It encompasses the structured aggregation of environment variables, active file paths, dependency trees, and executable tool schemas. Because language models operate within finite context windows, agents must dynamically select relevant context while filtering out noise. Standardizing context layouts prevents configuration warnings and enables predictable multi-turn execution.

slides.title: Recap: Model Context Protocol Core Primitives
bullets: MCP standardizes communication between agent clients and tool or context servers.
Resources provide readable data sources like source files, logs, and schemas.
Prompts offer predefined prompt templates for standardized workspace interactions.
Tools empower agents to run executable functions with specific input parameters.
slides.notes: The Model Context Protocol (MCP) establishes a standardized architecture for connecting language models to external tools and data sources. The three fundamental primitives defined by MCP are Resources, Prompts, and Tools. Resources allow the agent to read static or dynamic data such as repository files. Prompts provide structured templates. Tools define executable endpoints that produce side effects, such as running a test suite or invoking a static analyzer.

slides.title: Architecting Custom Tool Integrations
bullets: Tool integration exposes local dev utilities like linters and test runners to agents.
Agents invoke tools via JSON-RPC messages adhering to defined schema contracts.
Input schemas strictly define valid argument types to guarantee execution safety.
Server responses return formatted text or content blocks back to the agent context.
slides.notes: When an agent needs to execute an external command, such as invoking a linter or running unit tests, it generates a structured tool call. The host application intercepts this request, validates the arguments against the tool's JSON Schema definition, and forwards it to the tool server. The tool server executes the underlying script and returns JSON-formatted text back to the agent context. This pipeline keeps execution decoupled and safe.

slides.title: Configuring Agent Workspace Tool Specs
bullets: Workspace configuration files map MCP tool servers to agent environments.
Configurations define server entry points, command arguments, and environment variables.
Syntax errors or schema mismatches cause initialization warnings in static analyzers.
Passing public verification tests requires valid tool signatures and error handling.
slides.notes: To integrate custom tools, developers configure a JSON manifest or workspace configuration file that specifies how the agent host connects to tool servers. These configurations define executable paths, environment parameters, and tool capability declarations. If non-standard properties are included or schemas are malformed, static analyzers generate workspace warnings and public integration tests will fail during automated evaluation.

slides.title: Configuring an MCP Tool Server Step by Step
bullets: Step 1: Define the server executable and environment in workspace settings.
Step 2: Register valid tool definitions using name, description, and inputSchema.
Step 3: Handle tool execution requests and format structured responses.
Step 4: Run workspace static analysis to confirm zero configuration warnings.
slides.notes: Let me walk you through setting up an MCP tool server in your agent workspace. First, we add the server entry to our workspace configuration under mcpServers. We specify the binary command and argument paths. Next, within the server implementation, we declare tools with valid JSON Schemas. Finally, we run static analyzer checks to verify that the workspace configuration contains no unknown attributes or invalid JSON paths.

slides.notes: Let's check your understanding of MCP primitives. Remember that MCP standardizes interactions around Resources, Prompts, and Tools. When registering tools, using non-standard properties like outputSchema will result in configuration warnings from static analyzers.

slides.title: Validating Integrations and Resolving Warnings
bullets: Run public automated integration test suites to verify server handler logic.
Check static analyzer outputs to eliminate JSON configuration warnings.
Ensure tool response formats match standard MCP text and image content structures.
Verify test suite execution with JUnit or automated test harnesses.
slides.notes: Configuring custom tools requires double verification: static validation and dynamic testing. Static analyzers check that workspace configuration files and JSON Schemas conform strictly to the MCP specification without unknown properties. Integration test suites then invoke the server's tools with public test cases, ensuring that error handling, tool response payloads, and execution codes function correctly without throwing unhandled exceptions.

slides.title: Summary of Agent Workspaces and Tool Integrations
bullets: Context engineering delivers precise workspace information to coding agents.
MCP defines three core primitives: Resources, Prompts, and Tools.
Tool definitions must use standard fields: `name`, `description`, and `inputSchema`.
Valid configurations pass static analysis without warnings and satisfy all public tests.
slides.notes: To summarize today's lecture: context engineering is critical for enabling coding agents to reason about complex projects. The Model Context Protocol standardizes this via Resources, Prompts, and Tools. When constructing custom tools, adhere strictly to the MCP tool specification—avoiding non-standard attributes—so your workspace configurations validate cleanly and pass all automated tests.
